title: A full round

segments.voice: Yesterday, ajapa: the mantra that says itself, so on the in-breath, ham on the out. Your line was it says itself. Did you hear it underneath? Today, the end of mantra week, and your first full round. Day one hundred ten.

Pick up a mala, a string of prayer beads, anywhere in India, and count them. One hundred and eight. Plus one more, bigger, set apart, often with a tassel. Temples ring bells 108 times. Gods have 108 names, recited in a single long list. Sacred sites come in sets of 108. It's everywhere. Ask people why, and you'll get a dozen confident answers, and they won't match. Today you're going to do your first full round of 108. But first, the honest truth about the number.
screen: `108 BEADS, PLUS ONE.` → `108 NAMES, 108 BELLS.` → `A DOZEN ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Nobody knows for certain why 108. Here are some of the answers people give, and you can enjoy them without picking one. It's one, times two squared, times three cubed: one times four times twenty-seven. People love that. There's a traditional list of 108 Upanishads. The distance from the earth to the sun, some point out, is about 108 times the sun's width. Tradition gives 108 names for Vishnu, for Shiva, for the Goddess, for Ganesha. None of these is the origin, and the texts don't give one. What's clear is that the number means complete. A full circle. Now, how a round works. The big bead is called the meru, like the sacred mountain at the center of the world, or the guru bead. You start next to it. Hold the mala in your right hand, draped over the middle finger, and use your thumb to pull each bead toward you, one bead per mantra. Many teachers say to keep the index finger off the beads, pointing away. Some explain it as the finger of ego, but not every lineage says so. When you come back around to the meru, you don't cross it. You stop. If you want another round, you turn the mala around and go back the way you came. And that's the week. You found the one that fits. Bowed to Shiva's stillness. Asked Ganesha to clear the road. Sang the name. Held the Gayatri's light. Let the mantra say itself. Now, one full round. Complete is enough. 108 is enough.
screen: `NOBODY KNOWS FOR CERTAIN WHY.` · `IT MEANS COMPLETE.` · `THE MERU BEAD: DON'T CROSS IT.` · `THUMB PULLS, INDEX FINGER AWAY.` · then, large: `108 IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: 108. Pick your mantra: the one that fits, or Om, or Om Namah Shivaya. If you have a mala, start beside the big bead. If not, use your finger joints, twelve per hand counted with the thumb, nine times through. Begin, softly or silently. One bead, one mantra. The bell will ring before you finish, and that's fine. Keep going past it until you reach the meru. A full round usually takes five to ten minutes. When you're done, don't start another. Sit for three breaths. The bell holds the time.
108. The number of beads on a mala. Nobody knows exactly why, but everyone agrees it means complete.
Your line: 108 is enough. Today, finish one thing all the way round, a chore, a call, a page, and then stop. Don't start the next round. Day one hundred ten.

howItsDone: Hindus doing japa commonly use a mala of 108 beads plus a larger meru bead, moving one bead per mantra with the thumb and middle finger, and turning back at the meru rather than crossing it; one full round is 108 repetitions.

original.note: Sanskrit: a garland, and a string of prayer beads, usually 108 plus the meru.

trapdoor: what you thought: 108 is a magic number with one secret meaning.
what it means: nobody knows exactly why; what everyone agrees is that it means complete: one full round, and then stop.
what a scholar hears: 1 × 2² × 3³; the Muktika canon of 108 Upanishads; ashtottara shatanamavali, the 108-name lists; the explanations are many and none is the source.

notes: 'The distance from the earth to the sun is about 108 times the sun's width' — approximately true (about 107.5 solar diameters). Framed as 'some point out'. Keeper may prefer to drop it.
Mala technique (draped over the middle finger, thumb pulls, index finger kept away, not crossing the meru) varies by lineage. Confirm.

Finger-joint counting: 12 joints per hand (excluding thumbs) — a common method is counting 12 then tracking with the other hand; '12 per hand, nine times through' is the writer's simplification. Confirm.
Outline practice '108' exceeds the 2-minute sit; the practice invites continuing past the bell.
